§0Orientation

Ventilation & gas exchange

Move the air, then trade the gas — the physics of breathing.

This week is built in a deliberate order. First what the respiratory system does (§1); then the physical laws of fluid movement (§2) that everything else obeys; those laws applied to lung mechanics (§3) and to the volumes we can measure (§4); then gas diffusion (§5) — the actual exchange; and finally the ventilation–perfusion ratio (§6) that tells us, clinically, whether air and blood are meeting where they should.

Reasoning · why the laws come before the lungs

Breathing is just physics wearing anatomy. Boyle's law explains why the diaphragm dropping pulls air in; Poiseuille's law explains why a narrowed airway (asthma) chokes flow; partial-pressure gradients explain why oxygen crosses into blood at all. Learn the three laws in §2 and the rest of the week becomes their consequences — which is why we do the physics first.

R Recall checklist — orientation
  • Two jobs: ventilation (bulk movement of air) then gas exchange (diffusion between air and blood).
  • The order: functions → fluid-movement laws → lung mechanics → volumes/capacities → diffusion → V/Q.
  • Underlying physics: Boyle's law (mechanics), Poiseuille (resistance), partial pressures (diffusion).
§1Functions · LO1

The five functions of the respiratory system

Conduct, condition, exchange, buffer, and speak.

The respiratory system has five major functions: (1) conduct air to/from the alveoli, (2) condition & protect (warm, humidify, filter), (3) gas exchange with blood, (4) blood pH regulation, and (5) vocalisation. All but vocalisation serve (or result from) respiration. Note the distinction: external respiration is the bulk/diffusive movement of gases atmosphere↔lung↔blood↔cells; cellular respiration is the use of O₂ and production of CO₂ to make ATP.

§1.1Conduction of air

Air is moved in bulk through the upper tract (nasal & oral cavities, pharynx, larynx) and the lower tract (trachea → branching bronchi → lungs with alveoli). Only the lower tract is air-only (Plate 1.1).

Label Key — Upper airway & larynx
Nasal cavity
Warms, filters and adds smell; air-only route.
Mouth (oral cavity)
Shared air + food route.
Epiglottis
Elastic-cartilage 'trap door' that closes over the larynx when swallowing to keep food out of the trachea.
Vocal cords (true)
Elastic ligaments that vibrate as air passes — pitch = degree of stretch, loudness = air pressure.
Glottis / supraglottis / subglottis
The vocal-cord opening and the regions above and below it.
Trachea (windpipe)
The start of the lower, air-only conducting tract.
Clinical · the pharynx, the Eustachian tube and the epiglottis

The pharynx shares air and food and equalises middle-ear pressure via the Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube — which is why a cold blocks your ears and why swallowing 'pops' them on descent. The epiglottis is the airway's guard: when it fails (e.g. impaired swallowing after stroke), food enters the trachea → aspiration and pneumonia. The false vocal cords let you breath-hold to brace the trunk when lifting.

§1.2Conditioning, protection & surfactant

The respiratory mucosa conditions air before the alveoli: warming to 37 °C, humidifying to 100%, and filtering particles/pathogens. The mucociliary escalator (cilia beating on a thin saline layer) sweeps trapped mucus up and out.

But the mucosal fluid creates a problem: surface tension pulls the wet alveolar walls together. The pressure needed to hold an alveolus open follows Laplace's law — P = 2T / r — and if the fluid were pure water it would take ~18 cmH₂O. The fix is surfactant (Plate 1.2).

Label Key — Surfactant
Hydrophilic head
Sits in the alveolar fluid layer.
Hydrophobic tail
Projects into the alveolar air.
Made by alveolar (type II) cells
Half-life ~14 h; lines alveoli and small bronchioles.
Reduces surface tension
Lowers T in Laplace's law — so far less pressure is needed to keep alveoli open.
Worked example · Laplace's law and alveolar collapse

Why do small alveoli tend to collapse into large ones without surfactant?

  1. State the law: P = 2T / r — the pressure holding an alveolus open rises as radius (r) falls.
  2. For a fixed surface tension T, a smaller alveolus needs a higher pressure to stay open, so it tends to empty into a larger, lower-pressure one.
  3. Surfactant reduces T more at low volumes than at high — raising small-alveolus stability and equalising pressures (P ↓ = 2T ↓ / r).

Answer: surfactant's volume-dependent drop in surface tension prevents small alveoli collapsing — alveolar stability.

Clinical · neonatal respiratory distress syndrome

Surfactant is made late in fetal life, so premature infants can be born without enough. Their alveoli collapse on every breath (high surface tension), causing respiratory distress syndrome that needs immediate therapy (exogenous surfactant, respiratory support). A direct clinical payoff of Laplace's law.

§1.3Gas exchange & pH regulation

Gas exchange (function 3) moves O₂ from alveolar air into blood and CO₂ the other way — covered in depth in §5. pH regulation (function 4) rides on CO₂: dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which releases H⁺:

CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻  (via carbonic anhydrase)

So more CO₂ → more H⁺ → lower pH. By changing the rate of ventilation, the body blows off or retains CO₂ and thereby shifts blood pH.

Reasoning · why you breathe faster when your blood turns acidic

Because the CO₂ equation runs both ways, ventilation is a fast pH dial. Exercise or metabolic acid pushes the equation right (more H⁺); the body responds by increasing ventilation to blow off CO₂, dragging the equation back left and raising pH. It is the reason a breathless, hyperventilating patient may be compensating for an acidosis — the lungs are the rapid arm of acid–base balance (kidneys are the slow arm).

§1.4Vocalisation

Speech needs three things together: (1) air in motion (respiratory muscles + clear airways), (2) vibration of that airstream (the vocal cords), and (3) resonance shaping the buzz (throat, oral & nasal cavities).

R Recall checklist — respiratory functions
  • Five functions: conduct air · condition & protect · gas exchange · pH regulation · vocalisation.
  • Conduction — upper tract (nose, pharynx, larynx) + lower tract (trachea, bronchi, alveoli).
  • Conditioning — warm to 37 °C, humidify to 100%, filter; mucociliary clearance.
  • Surfactant (alveolar cells) lowers surface tension (Laplace P = 2T/r) → alveolar stability; lack → neonatal RDS.
  • pH — CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; ventilation rate tunes blood pH.
  • Vocalisation — air in motion + vocal-cord vibration + resonance.
§2Fluid movement · LO2

Key terms in fluid movement

Pressure drives flow; radius rules resistance.

Air (a fluid) moves in bulk flow from high to low pressure — exactly like water between two tanks. If lung pressure is below atmospheric, air flows in; above, air flows out; equal, no flow. Two laws quantify this: Boyle's (how pressure and volume trade) and Poiseuille's (what sets resistance).

§2.1Boyle's law — changing pressure by changing volume

Boyle's law: for a fixed mass of gas, pressure is inversely proportional to volume — P ∝ 1/V, i.e. P₁·V₁ = P₂·V₂ (Plate 2.1). This is the engine of breathing: increase lung volume → pressure drops below atmospheric → air flows in (inspiration); decrease volume → pressure rises above atmospheric → air flows out (exhalation).

Label Key — Boyle's law
V₁ = 1 L, P₁ = 100 mmHg
Starting state of a fixed mass of gas.
V₂ = 0.5 L, P₂ = 200 mmHg
Halve the volume and pressure doubles — the inverse relationship.
P₁·V₁ = P₂·V₂
The constant product; rearrange to find any unknown.
Link to breathing
Lungs expand → P falls → air in; lungs shrink → P rises → air out.
Worked example · Boyle's law

A fixed mass of air occupies 1 L at 100 mmHg. What is the pressure if the volume is compressed to 0.5 L?

  1. State the law: P₁·V₁ = P₂·V₂.
  2. Rearrange for P₂: P₂ = P₁·V₁ / V₂.
  3. Substitute: P₂ = (100 mmHg × 1 L) / 0.5 L = 200 mmHg — halving V doubled P.

Answer: 200 mmHg — pressure and volume are inversely proportional.

§2.2Resistance — Poiseuille's law

Airway resistance (R) follows the corollary of Poiseuille's law: R = 8μL / (π·r⁴), where μ = viscosity, L = tube length, r = radius. Since flow Q ∝ ΔP / R, a bigger radius means far less resistance and more flow; a longer tube means more resistance.

Reasoning · why radius is everything (the fourth power)

Resistance depends on radius to the fourth power (r⁴). Halve the radius and resistance rises 16-fold (2⁴), so flow collapses to 1/16. That is why a small amount of airway narrowing — bronchospasm in asthma, mucosal swelling, a mucus plug — causes such a dramatic drop in airflow, and why bronchodilators (widening r) are so effective. To increase flow: increase diameter, decrease length.

§2.3Where the resistance actually is

Counter-intuitively, the tiny alveoli are the site of lowest resistance. As the airways branch, their combined cross-sectional area becomes enormous, so total resistance falls and velocity slows — perfect for gas exchange. Air moves fast through the trachea/bronchi (bulk flow) but almost stops at the alveoli (largest total cross-section, lowest resistance) where diffusion takes over.

Memory hook · the three laws of the airway

Boyle blows the air in and out (P·V). Poiseuille pinches the flow (r⁴ resistance). Partial pressures pull the gases across (§5). Mechanics, resistance, diffusion.

R Recall checklist — fluid movement
  • Air is a fluid; it moves in bulk flow from high to low pressure.
  • Boyle's law — P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; expanding the lungs lowers pressure → inspiration.
  • Poiseuille — R = 8μL/πr⁴; resistance depends on radius⁴, so small narrowing = big flow loss (asthma).
  • Flow Q ∝ ΔP/R; increase radius or shorten the tube to increase flow.
  • Lowest resistance is at the alveoli (largest total cross-sectional area) — where diffusion happens.
§3Lung mechanics · LO3

Lung mechanics — pressure & volume in a breath

Muscles change the volume; Boyle's law does the rest.

Inspiration is active (Plate 3.1): the diaphragm contracts and flattens downward, while the external intercostals and scalenes pull the ribs up and out — both enlarge the thorax. Exhalation is nominally passive (muscles relax and the elastic lung recoils), but forced exhalation adds the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles (which push the viscera and diaphragm upward).

Label Key — Muscles of inspiration
Diaphragm
The main inspiratory muscle; contracts and flattens downward to enlarge the thorax.
External intercostals
Pull the ribs up and out (a 'bucket-handle' rise).
Scalenes
Accessory muscles that lift the upper ribs.
Result
Thoracic volume ↑ → intrapleural & alveolar pressure ↓ → air flows in (Boyle).
Reasoning · why the negative intrapleural pressure is the crucial link

Lung tissue has no muscle — it is elastic and cannot expand itself. It follows the chest wall only because the pleural fluid between the two pleural layers is cohesive (like two wet glass slides that slide but won't separate). The intrapleural pressure is negative at rest; when the thorax expands it becomes more negative, and that suction is partially transmitted to the lung, dropping alveolar pressure below atmospheric so air flows in. Break the seal (a hole in the pleura) and the lung recoils away from the wall — a pneumothorax.

Over one respiratory cycle, alveolar pressure (PA) swings below then above atmospheric pressure (Patm) while intrapleural pressure stays negative (Plate 3.2). At the end of exhalation, airflow ceases when PA again equals Patm.

Label Key — Pressures in a breath
Intrapleural pressure
Negative throughout; becomes more negative during inspiration.
Alveolar pressure (P_A)
Falls below atmospheric in inspiration (air in), rises above it in exhalation (air out).
Airflow
Follows the P_A–P_atm difference; zero when they are equal.
One cycle
= one inspiration + one exhalation.
Clinical · pneumothorax

Because the lung is held out only by the negative intrapleural pressure, a penetrating chest wound or a ruptured bleb lets air into the pleural space (pneumothorax). The pressure equalises, the elastic lung collapses inward, and ventilation of that lung fails — a direct consequence of losing the negative intrapleural pressure.

R Recall checklist — lung mechanics
  • Inspiration (active) — diaphragm flattens down; external intercostals + scalenes lift ribs up/out → volume ↑.
  • Exhalation — usually passive (elastic recoil); forced adds internal intercostals + abdominals.
  • Intrapleural pressure is negative; pleural-fluid cohesion makes the elastic lung follow the chest wall.
  • Inspiration makes intrapleural pressure more negative → alveolar pressure < atmospheric → air in (Boyle).
  • Lose the seal → pneumothorax (lung collapses).
§4Volumes & capacities · LO4

Pulmonary volumes & capacities

Four volumes that don't overlap; four capacities that add them up.

A spirometry trace splits lung air into four volumes (which never overlap) and four capacities (each a sum of volumes) (Plate 4.1).

Label Key — Volumes & capacities
Tidal volume (TV)
Air in/out of one normal breath (~0.5 L).
Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV)
Extra air inhaled beyond a tidal breath (~3 L).
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV)
Extra air exhaled beyond a tidal breath (~1.1 L).
Residual volume (RV)
Air left after maximal exhalation (~1.2 L) — cannot be exhaled.
Capacities
IC = TV+IRV · FRC = ERV+RV · VC = TV+IRV+ERV · TLC = VC+RV.
The four volumes and four capacities
TermDefinitionAdult value
Tidal volume (TV)One normal breath in or out~0.5 L
Inspiratory reserve (IRV)Max extra inhaled above TV~3 L
Expiratory reserve (ERV)Max extra exhaled below TV~1.1 L
Residual volume (RV)Air left after maximal exhalation~1.2 L
Inspiratory capacity (IC)TV + IRV~3.5 L
Functional residual capacity (FRC)ERV + RV~2.3 L
Vital capacity (VC)TV + IRV + ERV~4.6 L
Total lung capacity (TLC)VC + RV~5.8 L
Reasoning · why residual volume can never be measured by spirometry

A capacity is just a sum of volumes — but any capacity that includes residual volume (FRC, TLC) can't be measured by simple spirometry, because RV is the air you cannot exhale, so it never crosses the spirometer. That is why RV, FRC and TLC need indirect methods (helium dilution, body plethysmography) — a favourite exam point.

§4.1Minute ventilation

The rate air moves through the lungs is the minute ventilation (minute respiratory volume, V̇): V̇ = VT × RR (tidal volume × respiratory rate). It matters more than tidal volume or rate alone.

Worked example · minute ventilation & vital capacity

An adult breathes a tidal volume of 0.5 L at 12 breaths/min, with IRV 3 L and ERV 1.1 L. Find minute ventilation and vital capacity.

  1. Minute ventilation: V̇ = V_T × RR = 0.5 L × 12 = 6 L/min.
  2. Vital capacity: VC = TV + IRV + ERV = 0.5 + 3 + 1.1 = 4.6 L.
  3. Note: doubling either rate or depth doubles V̇ — but deeper breaths waste less on dead space.

Answer: minute ventilation ≈ 6 L/min; vital capacity ≈ 4.6 L.

R Recall checklist — volumes & capacities
  • Four volumes (no overlap): TV (~0.5 L), IRV (~3 L), ERV (~1.1 L), RV (~1.2 L).
  • Four capacities (sums): IC = TV+IRV; FRC = ERV+RV; VC = TV+IRV+ERV; TLC = VC+RV.
  • Residual volume can't be exhaled → capacities containing RV (FRC, TLC) need indirect measurement.
  • Minute ventilation V̇ = V_T × RR (e.g. 0.5 L × 12 = 6 L/min).
§5Gas diffusion · LO5

Gas diffusion across the membrane

Bulk flow gets air to the alveolus; diffusion moves gas into blood.

Two different transports: bulk flow moves the whole air mixture into the alveoli (§2–3); diffusion then moves individual gases across the alveolar–capillary membrane, driven by each gas's partial-pressure gradient (Plate 5.1). O₂ diffuses from high alveolar pO₂ into blood; CO₂ diffuses the other way.

Label Key — Alveolar–capillary exchange
Alveolus
Air-filled sac; source of O₂ and sink for CO₂.
Capillary (~1 RBC wide)
Dense network; blood in (deoxygenated) → blood out (oxygenated).
O₂ in
Diffuses down its partial-pressure gradient from alveolus to blood.
CO₂ out
Diffuses the opposite way, from blood to alveolus.
Not pumped
Exchange is pure diffusion — no active transport across the membrane.

The rate of diffusion depends on several factors (a Fick relationship): D ≈ (ΔP × A × S) / (d × √MW) — partial-pressure difference (ΔP), area (A), gas solubility (S), membrane distance (d) and molecular weight (MW). For normal healthy lungs the dominant term is the partial-pressure difference (ΔP).

Reasoning · why disease attacks the other terms

In health, ΔP rules. In disease, the anatomical terms dominate: emphysema destroys alveolar walls (↓ area A), pulmonary fibrosis or oedema thickens the membrane (↑ distance d), and altitude or hypoventilation lowers alveolar pO₂ (↓ ΔP). Reading the Fick equation tells you exactly which diseases impair gas exchange and how.

§5.1Dalton's law & the partial pressures of air

Dalton's law: the total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its components. Using it, we can find the pO₂ of dry vs humid (lung) air — note that humidifying lowers pO₂ because water vapour claims some of the pressure.

Partial pressures in dry vs 100% humid air (Dalton's law)
Dry air100% humid air (lungs)
Atmospheric pressure760 mmHg760 mmHg
Water vapour pressure0 mmHg47 mmHg (≈24 in slide's example)
Gas pressure (atmospheric − vapour)760 mmHg736 mmHg
pO₂ (21% of gas pressure)~160 mmHg~155 mmHg
pCO₂ (0.033%)~0.25 mmHg~0.24 mmHg
Worked example · partial pressure with Dalton's law

Atmospheric pressure is 760 mmHg and oxygen is 21% of the gas. Find pO₂ in dry air and in 100%-humid lung air (water vapour 24 mmHg).

  1. Dry air: gas pressure = 760 mmHg, so pO₂ = 0.21 × 760 = ~160 mmHg.
  2. Humid air: first subtract water vapour — gas pressure = 760 − 24 = 736 mmHg.
  3. Then pO₂ = 0.21 × 736 = ~155 mmHg — humidifying slightly lowers pO₂.

Answer: pO₂ ≈ 160 mmHg (dry) vs ~155 mmHg (humid lung air).

Because gas always flows high→low partial pressure, oxygen descends a cascade from atmosphere → alveolus → blood → mitochondria (Plate 5.2), while CO₂ runs the reverse cascade from tissues → atmosphere (Plate 5.3). Increasing ventilation raises alveolar pO₂ (and lowers pCO₂), increasing diffusion in both directions (Plate 5.4).

Label Key — The oxygen cascade
Atmosphere (highest pO₂)
~160 mmHg — the top of the cascade.
Alveolus → arterial blood
pO₂ drops with humidification, mixing and diffusion.
Tissues → mitochondria (lowest)
The sink — oxygen flows down the whole gradient to be used.
Principle
Gas flows high → low partial pressure at every step.
Label Key — CO₂ movement
Venous blood (highest pCO₂)
CO₂ produced by tissues raises venous pCO₂.
Alveolus → trachea → atmosphere
CO₂ diffuses and is ventilated out down its gradient.
Opposite direction to O₂
Same partial-pressure principle, reversed.
Label Key — Ventilation & O₂ uptake
↑ ventilation
Raises alveolar pO₂...
↑ alveolar pO₂
...which increases the ΔP for O₂ diffusion into blood.
Rest vs exercise
O₂ absorption rises with ventilation to meet demand.
R Recall checklist — gas diffusion
  • Bulk flow fills the alveolus; diffusion moves individual gases across the membrane down partial-pressure gradients.
  • Diffusion rate D ≈ (ΔP × A × S)/(d × √MW); in health ΔP dominates.
  • Disease hits area (emphysema ↓A), distance (fibrosis/oedema ↑d) or ΔP.
  • Dalton's law — total P = sum of partial pressures; humid lung air pO₂ ~155 vs dry ~160 mmHg.
  • Oxygen cascade atmosphere→mitochondria; CO₂ runs the reverse; ↑ventilation ↑ diffusion.
§6V/Q ratio · LO6

The ventilation–perfusion ratio

Gas exchange needs air and blood meeting — V/Q measures the match.

Good gas exchange needs both ventilation (air) and perfusion (blood) at the same alveoli. The ventilation–perfusion ratio quantifies the match: V/Q = V̇A / Q̇ (alveolar ventilation ÷ blood flow).

  • ↑ ventilation raises alveolar pO₂, increasing O₂ diffusion in and CO₂ out.
  • ↑ perfusion raises the effective blood 'surface area' exposed for exchange.

§6.1The two extremes

The extremes show why both are needed:

  • V/Q = 0 (no ventilation): alveolar gas equilibrates with venous blood; no partial-pressure difference → no exchange. Blood passes without being oxygenated — a shunt.
  • V/Q → ∞ (no perfusion): ventilated but no blood to load the gas; the stagnant blood equilibrates and no net exchange occurs — dead space.
Reasoning · why the normal ratio is ~0.8, not 1

One litre of blood carries ~200 mL O₂ and one litre of air holds ~210 mL O₂, so the 'ideal' ratio would be ~1. But regional differences in the lung pull the real average down to about 0.8 — which also matches the physiology: normal alveolar ventilation ≈ 4 L/min and cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min, and 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8.

Worked example · the normal V/Q ratio

Alveolar ventilation is ~4 L/min and cardiac output (perfusion) is ~5 L/min. What is the V/Q ratio?

  1. Definition: V/Q = V̇_A / Q̇.
  2. Substitute: V/Q = 4 L/min ÷ 5 L/min.
  3. Simplify: V/Q = 0.8 — the normal whole-lung average.

Answer: ~0.8, consistent with air/blood O₂ contents and with normal ventilation vs cardiac output.

§6.2Clinical use

Abnormal V/Q and its causes
RatioMeaningSeen in
Low V/QLow ventilation (or high perfusion) — poorly ventilated alveoliAsthma; chronic bronchitis; acute pulmonary oedema
High V/QHigh ventilation (or low perfusion) — poorly perfused alveoliPulmonary embolism (↓ perfusion); emphysema (↑ ventilation to compensate for damage)
Clinical · V/Q as a diagnostic lens

A low V/Q means air isn't getting in (obstruction/fluid): asthma, chronic bronchitis, pulmonary oedema. A high V/Q means blood isn't getting through: classically pulmonary embolism (a clot blocks perfusion → ventilated but unperfused dead space). The concept returns in the unit's work on exercise homeostasis and COPD — it is the single number that tells you whether the lung's two supply lines are matched.

Memory hook · V/Q extremes

V/Q = 0 → shunt (blood, no air — like breath-holding while your heart beats). V/Q = ∞ → dead space (air, no blood — like a PE). Zero = shunt, infinity = dead space.

R Recall checklist — ventilation-perfusion ratio
  • V/Q = V̇_A / Q̇ — alveolar ventilation ÷ perfusion; measures air–blood matching.
  • V/Q = 0 → shunt (perfused, not ventilated); V/Q = ∞ → dead space (ventilated, not perfused).
  • Normal ≈ 0.8 (≈ 4 L/min ventilation ÷ 5 L/min cardiac output).
  • Low V/Q — asthma, chronic bronchitis, pulmonary oedema; high V/Q — pulmonary embolism, emphysema.
